title: Rosalind and the Safehouse
premise: Quentin Ishikawa, a veteran interpreter for a collapsing peace delegation, discovers her own voiceprint is the encryption key to a server holding twenty years of diplomatic blackmail — recordings she never made, in her own voice. The server was built by her late mother, a translator whose death was ruled an accident, and its contents could indict officials in three governments. Hunted by an assassin who only kills people who 'stop existing' in official records, Quentin must smuggle the archive across a border whose checkpoints change shifts at dawn, trading her carefully constructed identity for the truth of who her mother was and what Quentin herself was recruited to become. In the end she delivers the archive not to a government but to the delegation itself, forcing the peace talks to fail loudly rather than succeed quietly, and crosses the border under her mother's name — alive, documented, and finally her own person.
about_author: Petra Thornbury is the pen name of a former conference interpreter who spent a decade in negotiation rooms across three continents before turning to fiction. She writes thrillers about people whose professional gift — being believed in every language — becomes their greatest liability.

chapters.title: Consecutive
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. During the final session of a doomed peace delegation, Quentin interprets a speech she knows is a lie and notices a delegate mouthing her name. The emotional beat is weary professionalism cracking into unease — twenty years of rules, and tonight one of them is being broken around her.

chapters.title: The Voiceprint
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. A courier slips her a battered phone; a recorded prompt asks her to speak, and a server in another continent unlocks. The files are indexed by dates from her childhood. Beat: vertigo — her voice opening doors she never built.

chapters.title: What Mother Left
chapters.summary: POV Quentin, with a flashback to age nine. She deciphers the archive's structure and finds her mother's death certificate dated three days after a recording of her mother's voice — alive — on the server. Beat: grief re-opened as a live investigation.

chapters.title: The Man Who Isn't There
chapters.summary: POV the assassin, Voss. He reviews a kill list and finds Quentin's name flagged for 'record dissolution' — erasure, not murder. Beat: cold procedure, with one flicker of curiosity about a target who doesn't know she's already been deleted.

chapters.title: Rules of Engagement
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. She tests the delegation's security chief, Aldous, and realizes he already knows about the server — and is deciding whether she's an asset or a leak. Beat: the interpreter becomes the interpreted.

chapters.title: Three Governments, One Lie
chapters.summary: POV Quentin, intercut with a minister's aide burning documents. The recordings implicate officials in all three negotiating states; the peace deal is the payment for silence. Beat: betrayal at institutional scale, personal stakes sharpening.

chapters.title: Shift Change
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. She learns the border checkpoint rotates guards at dawn and that the rotation is the only window when her dissolved records won't flag. Beat: a plan forms — fragile, clock-bound, hers for the first time.

chapters.title: Voss Calls
chapters.summary: POV Voss. He contacts Quentin not to kill her but to verify she exists — his contract requires confirmation before dissolution, and her voiceprint has confused his systems. Beat: eerie professional courtesy masking mutual threat.

chapters.title: The Delegation Fails on Schedule
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. The talks collapse exactly as the recordings predicted; Aldous offers her extraction in exchange for the archive. Beat: the temptation of safety at the price of the truth.

chapters.title: Mother's Grammar
chapters.summary: POV Quentin, deep flashback. Young Quentin learns her mother hid messages inside translation exercises — the server's folder names are old homework. Beat: tenderness and fury braided; inheritance revealed as instruction.

chapters.title: Burn the Interpreter
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Her accreditation is revoked; hotel key stops working; colleagues look through her. Voss's dissolution has begun. Beat: terror of unpersoning — identity stripped to its studs.

chapters.title: Aldous's Choice
chapters.summary: POV Aldous. Torn between the service that owns him and the interpreter who trusted him, he passes her the checkpoint rotation roster and lies to his handlers. Beat: a minor character earns his redemption at real cost.

chapters.title: Night Bus to the Line
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. She travels toward the border with the archive on three redundant drives, spotting Voss's surveillance shadow. Beat: dread sharpening into resolve; she stops running and starts maneuvering.

chapters.title: The Recording of Me
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. On the bus she plays the final file: her mother's voice explaining that the voiceprint key was Quentin herself — recruited at nine, unknowing, as the failsafe. Beat: the theme lands — she was the inheritance.

chapters.title: Checkpoint, Pre-Dawn
chapters.summary: POV Quentin and Voss alternating. Both arrive early for the shift change; a third party — the aide from chapter 6 — arrives to destroy the archive at the source relay. Beat: three clocks converging on one booth.

chapters.title: Interpreting the Assassin
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. She talks Voss through the checkpoint in three languages, turning his verification protocol against his employers — proving she exists so loudly his systems refuse the dissolution order. Beat: climax of wit; language as weapon.

chapters.title: What the Booth Saw
chapters.summary: POV Voss. His contract collapses; he makes his own choice and lets the aide's sabotage fail, walking away from the list. Beat: the hunter's cold architecture finally cracks into a human decision.

chapters.title: The Delegation, Interrupted
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Instead of fleeing, she walks the archive into the ruins of the talks and interprets her mother's recordings aloud to the delegations — the truth delivered in every language at once. Beat: the climax; failure made loud and undeniable.

chapters.title: Aftermath in Three Capitals
chapters.summary: POV Quentin, epistolary fragments. Resignations cascade; two governments spin, one falls; Quentin's records are restored — but under which name? Beat: exhausted triumph, the cost tallied.

chapters.title: The Question of Names
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Offered reinstatement, protection, and silence, she declines all three; Aldous, disgraced but free, gives her one honest piece of advice. Beat: quiet reckoning with identity as choice, not assignment.

chapters.title: Crossing
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. At dawn she crosses the checkpoint under her mother's restored name, papers genuine for the first time in her life, Voss watching from the crowd and nodding once. Beat: release — the border that was a threat becomes a threshold.

chapters.title: Simultaneous
chapters.summary: POV Quentin, months later. Working freelance in a small coastal city, she finishes translating her mother's letters and speaks the last one aloud to the empty room — the server's final file, meant for her alone. Beat: resolution; memory inherited, identity authored.
